messages.content:
Rate the following clinical vignette:

He grows up in a home where fear arrives before language does. As a child in an African household marked by strictness and volatility, he learns early that the caregiver who is supposed to protect him can also become the source of pain. The abuse is physical and unpredictable. It comes in slaps, blows, and punishments that feel larger than his small body can understand. He describes himself as always listening for changes in footsteps, the sound of a door opening, the tone in an adult's voice. Even now, he says that as a boy he becomes expert at reading the room, because noticing danger quickly is the only way he can prepare. He does not have words for what is happening then. He only knows that his body tightens, his stomach knots, and he tries to make himself smaller.

He carries that vigilance into adolescence and beyond. He learns to stay quiet, to avoid attention, to keep his face neutral. When other children argue or play roughly, he reacts as if something worse is about to happen. He remembers being teased for flinching, for tensing when someone reaches toward him too fast. Over time, he becomes someone who expects impact. He does not trust calm to last. In his family, affection and discipline remain tangled together, and he grows up unsure whether closeness means safety or exposure.

As an adult, he is 27, single, and working long hours as a taxi and Uber driver. The job suits parts of him because he is on the move, in control of the route, able to keep distance while still being around people. He likes the structure of picking someone up, dropping them off, and moving on. But driving also keeps him trapped with his thoughts. In the quiet between rides, memories come back without warning: a particular smell, the slam of a car door, the sharp edge of a passenger's voice, and suddenly he is not in his vehicle anymore but back in the household where he was hurt. He describes feeling as though his body does not understand that the danger is over. His shoulders stay raised. His jaw stays clenched. He checks mirrors constantly, scans for threats, and becomes irritated when another driver cuts him off or a passenger starts shouting directions.

He notices that he is easily startled. A hand on the car window, a sudden laugh in the back seat, even a vibration from his phone can send a wave of panic through him. He may grip the steering wheel until his knuckles ache. Sometimes his chest feels tight and his breathing short, and he has to remind himself to keep driving safely. At night, after he has finished work, he often avoids going straight home because the silence of his room makes everything louder. When he does sleep, it is broken. He wakes with his heart racing, drenched in sweat, sometimes from dreams that leave him confused and angry but unable to recall all the details. In the morning he feels drained, as if he has been working all night in a fight he cannot win.

He is careful with people, especially authority figures and older men, because they trigger memories of being powerless. He wants connection, but he also expects disappointment or harm. In relationships, he keeps things casual and guarded. He says it is easier not to depend on anyone. When he feels criticized, even mildly, shame rises fast and he can become withdrawn or defensive. He often tells himself that if he stays useful, calm, and hard to read, he will remain safe. Yet this effort is exhausting. He spends much of his day monitoring other people's moods, anticipating problems, replaying conversations, and imagining what he should have said differently. At times he feels disconnected from his own life, as though he is moving through it on autopilot, one ride after another.

Despite this, there are moments when he shows clear determination. He values his independence and takes pride in earning his own money. He likes arriving where he says he will arrive, keeping his car clean, and handling difficult passengers without losing control. Still, underneath that competence is a young man who continues to carry the household violence of his childhood in his body. The past is never far from the present; it lives in the way he flinches, watches, holds himself tense, and keeps driving as if staying in motion might be the only way to stay ahead of what he remembers.

output.reasoning: The sentence 'At night, after he has finished work, he often avoids going straight home because the silence of his room makes everything louder' explicitly shows avoidance of an external reminder (his home) that would trigger trauma-related memories and feelings. This clearly demonstrates DSM-5 Criterion C.
output.rationale: The vignette includes explicit avoidance behavior of a place (home) that triggers trauma-related thoughts and feelings.
